lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a business you can start now
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a business idea that fits your skills, money and situation.
This lesson builds toward: Given your skills and the money you could start with, you will choose a business idea that fits your skills, money and situation, with low startup costs and any required state license checked.
The best first business is often simple: a service you already know how to do, that needs little money to start, and that people in your area pay for. Examples: house or office cleaning, lawn care, pressure washing, junk hauling, moving help, car detailing, painting, cooking, hair, sewing or repairs.
Ask an AI assistant to help you think: "I learned cooking and cleaning skills and I have about $300 to start. I do not have a car yet. Suggest five small service businesses I could start in my city, with what each needs to begin."
Some jobs need a state license, such as barbering, cosmetology, electrical or contracting work, and some licensing boards have rules about people with records. Before you choose one of these, check your state licensing board's official website or ask a reentry program. Many states have changed these rules, so do not assume you are blocked.
Step by step:
- List your skills and what you enjoy.
- Note your startup money and tools, such as a car.
- Ask AI for a few matching business ideas.
- Check whether an idea needs a state license.
- Pick one idea to plan.
Words to know:
- Service business: a business that does work for people, such as cleaning or repairs, instead of selling products.
- Startup costs: the money you need to begin, such as tools and supplies.
- Licensing board: the state office that gives licenses for some jobs.
Try it now: Write your top three skills and how much money you could start with. Ask an AI assistant for five matching small business ideas, then pick one.
You can now choose a small business idea that fits your skills and money.

options: The money needed to begin, such as tools and supplies
check.why: Startup costs are what you spend to get the business going.

check.q: You want to start a business doing electrical repairs. What would you do first?
options: Ask AI if you need a license and trust the answer
Check your state licensing board's official website
check.why: Many trades need a state license, and the official board has the real rules.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Customers and pricing
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe your customers and set a starting price that covers your costs.
This lesson builds toward: Given your business idea, you will describe your customers and set a starting price, with a specific customer sentence and a price that covers costs, time and taxes.
A business needs customers who will pay. Be specific about who they are: "busy families in my neighborhood", "small offices downtown", "older homeowners who cannot mow". Knowing them tells you where to find them.
To set a price, add up your costs for one job (supplies, gas or bus fare, and your time), then look at what others nearby charge. Ask AI: "I want to offer basic home cleaning in Atlanta. My supplies cost about $10 per job and a job takes 3 hours. How could I work out a fair starting price? What do I need to check about local prices?" Then check real local prices by looking at local ads or calling a few businesses.
Do not price so low that you lose money. A price should pay for your costs, your time, and a little extra for taxes and savings.
Step by step:
- Describe your customers in one sentence.
- Add up your costs for one job.
- Decide what your time is worth per hour.
- Check what others nearby charge.
- Set a price that covers costs, time and taxes.
Words to know:
- Customer: a person or business that pays for your service.
- Profit: the money left after you pay your costs.
Try it now: For your idea, write one sentence describing your customers. Ask AI to help you work out a starting price from your costs and time, then check two real local prices.
You can now describe your customers and set a starting price that covers your costs.

options: All the money customers pay you
check.why: Profit is what remains after you pay your costs.

check.q: AI suggests a lawn-care price that seems very low. What would you do?
options: Use it to get more customers
Ask friends to guess a price
Check your costs and time, then compare two real local prices
check.why: A price must cover your costs and time, and local prices show what customers pay.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: A one-page business plan with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page business plan with an AI assistant.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant that asks you questions, you will write a one-page business plan, covering service, customers, price, how customers find you and startup costs, with facts supplied by you.
A business plan is your map. The SBA describes a short "lean startup" plan that fits on one page, covering things like your customers, the value you offer, how you reach customers, your costs and how you make money.
Ask AI: "Help me write a one-page business plan for a lawn care business in my town. Use these headings: what I offer, who my customers are, why they would choose me, how they will find me, startup costs, price, and my first-month goal. Ask me questions one at a time to fill it in." Answer in your own words.
Read the finished plan carefully. Change anything that is not true or not realistic. You can show it to a mentor; SCORE offers free mentoring (see Lesson 6).
Step by step:
- Ask AI to interview you one question at a time.
- Use simple headings: offer, customers, why you, how they find you, costs, price, first goal.
- Answer in your own words.
- Fix anything unrealistic.
- Save it and share it with a mentor.
Words to know:
- Business plan: a written plan for how your business will work and make money.
- Lean startup plan: a short, one-page business plan.
Official sources:
- SBA: Write your business plan
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to interview you one question at a time and write a one-page plan for your business idea. Save the plan.
You can now write a one-page business plan with AI help.

check.q: What is a lean startup business plan?
check.why: A lean plan fits the key parts of a business on one page.

check.q: AI wrote your plan and added a customer number you never gave it. What would you do?
options: Remove or replace it with your real facts
Keep it because it looks good
Send the plan to a lender as it is
check.why: You supply the facts in your plan, not the AI.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Setting it up the official way

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Business structure and business name
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose a business structure and find out whether your business name needs to be registered.
This lesson builds toward: Given your business idea and name, you will choose a business structure and find whether your name needs a DBA, with the reason for your choice and the official government page found.
The SBA explains that if you start doing business without registering as another type, you are automatically a sole proprietorship. It is the simplest: you and the business are the same for taxes and debts, so you are personally responsible for the business's debts.
A limited liability company (LLC) is registered with your state, usually through the Secretary of State, and generally protects your personal belongings if the business is sued or goes into debt, though that protection has limits. It costs money to form and may have yearly fees, which differ by state; check your Secretary of State's website for the current cost.
If you use a business name that is not your own legal name, such as "Fresh Start Cleaning", most states require you to register it as a DBA ("doing business as") with the state, county or city. If you do business under your own legal name, the SBA says you may not need to register anywhere. Ask a tax professional or SBA partner which structure fits you.
Step by step:
- Decide: sole proprietorship (automatic) or LLC (registered with the state).
- For an LLC, check costs on your Secretary of State's website.
- Choose a business name.
- If it is not your legal name, find out where to register a DBA in your state, county or city.
- Ask a tax professional or SBA partner if unsure.
Words to know:
- Sole proprietorship: a business owned by one person, with no separation between the owner and the business.
- LLC: limited liability company: a registered business that generally protects the owner's personal belongings.
- DBA: "doing business as": a registered business name that is not your legal name.
Official sources:
- SBA: Choose a business structure
- SBA: Register your business
Try it now: Decide whether you would start as a sole proprietorship or an LLC, and write why. Choose a business name, then search "register DBA" plus your county or state and find the official government page (often ending in .gov).
You can now choose a business structure and find out how to register your business name.

check.why: DBA means doing business as, a name different from your legal name.

check.q: You want to call your business "Shine Car Care". What would you do?
options: Search for your county or state's official DBA page
Pay a random website to register it
Ask AI to register it for you
check.why: Most states require registering a business name that is not your legal name, on an official site.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Your free EIN and the right licenses
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find the free IRS EIN application and the licenses and permits your business needs.
This lesson builds toward: Using irs.gov and your local government sites, you will find the free EIN application and the licenses your business needs, with the official web address for each, and no paid EIN service.
An EIN (Employer Identification Number) is a tax ID number for your business. The IRS says "You never have to pay a fee for an EIN", and warns about websites that charge for one. Apply directly on irs.gov. If approved, the number is issued right away online. You must finish in one session, so set aside time; the online tool is only open at certain hours, listed on irs.gov. Sole proprietors without employees can often use their Social Security number instead, but many open an EIN to keep business and personal separate.
Licenses and permits come from different levels of government. The SBA explains that federal licenses are only for certain activities (such as alcohol or aviation); states license many trades; and cities and counties often require a general business license and permits for things like food, construction or vending.
To find yours: check your city and county websites for a business license, your state's website for trade licenses and sales tax registration if you sell products, and ask your local Small Business Development Center. Type your real numbers only on the official .gov sites, never into AI.
Step by step:
- Go to irs.gov and search "apply for an EIN"; never pay a website for one.
- Check the online hours and finish in one session.
- Print or save your EIN confirmation.
- Check your city and county for a business license and permits.
- Check your state for trade licenses and sales tax registration.
Words to know:
- EIN: Employer Identification Number: a free tax ID number for a business from the IRS.
- License: official permission from the government to run a business or do certain work.
- Permit: official permission for a specific activity, such as selling food.
Official sources:
- IRS: Get an employer identification number
- SBA: Apply for licenses and permits
Try it now: Open the IRS EIN page on irs.gov and write down the online hours and what you need to apply (do not apply yet unless you are ready). Then find your city or county's business license page and write down its web address.
You can now get a free EIN from the IRS and find the licenses and permits your business needs.

check.q: Where does a general business license usually come from?
check.why: General business licenses are usually issued by your city or county.

check.q: A website offers to get you an EIN for $150. What would you do?
options: Pay it because it is faster
Ask a friend to pay it
check.why: The IRS gives EINs for free on its own website.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Bank account, records, taxes and free help
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set up simple money records, plan for taxes, and find free business help.
This lesson builds toward: Given a new business, you will plan a separate bank account, simple records, money for taxes and free help, with a record log that has date, who, what and how much, and your nearest SCORE or SBDC named.
Keep business money separate. The SBA recommends opening a business bank account once you start taking in or spending money for the business. Banks commonly ask for an EIN (or your Social Security number for a sole proprietorship), formation documents and a business license; ask your bank what it needs.
Keep records of every dollar in and out: a simple spreadsheet or notebook with the date, who, what and how much, plus receipts. AI can design a simple record sheet for you: "Make me a simple income and expense log for a cleaning business." Do not paste real bank details into it.
Taxes: the IRS says self-employed people must file a tax return if net earnings are $400 or more, and generally pay self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare) as well as income tax, often as quarterly estimated payments. Forms include Schedule C, Schedule SE and Form 1040-ES. Many owners set aside part of each payment for taxes; a tax professional or free tax help can tell you how much. Free business help: SCORE offers volunteer mentors at no cost, and Small Business Development Centers and Women's Business Centers offer counseling; find them on sba.gov.
Step by step:
- Open a separate business bank account; ask the bank what it needs.
- Keep a log of every dollar in and out, with receipts.
- Set aside part of each payment for taxes.
- Learn the forms: Schedule C, Schedule SE, 1040-ES on irs.gov.
- Get free help from SCORE, an SBDC or a Women's Business Center.
Words to know:
- Self-employment tax: Social Security and Medicare tax that self-employed people pay.
- Estimated tax: tax paid during the year, usually every quarter, when no employer withholds it.
- Expense: money you spend to run the business.
Official sources:
- SBA: Open a business bank account
- IRS: Self-employed individuals tax center
- SBA: Resource partners
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page plan and make your setup checklist with an official website for each step: structure, name and DBA, free EIN on irs.gov, city, county and state licenses, a separate bank account, a record log made with AI, money set aside for taxes, and your nearest SCORE or SBDC.
You can now plan a small business and set it up the official way, with records, a tax plan and free help.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds One-page plan The plan is missing a part, or has facts the learner did not give. One page covering service, customers, price, how customers find you and startup costs. The learner can explain each part of the plan in their own words. Customers and price Customers are "everyone", or the price does not cover costs. A specific customer description and a price that covers costs, time and taxes. The price was compared with two real local prices. Structure and name No structure chosen, or the name was not checked. Structure chosen with a reason, and the official DBA page found if needed. Also notes where to check the current cost of forming an LLC. EIN and licenses Uses a paid EIN service, or no license check. irs.gov EIN page and city, county and state license pages listed. Notes the EIN online hours and what to have ready to apply. Money, records and help No separate account or record plan. A separate bank account, a record log, money set aside for taxes, and a SCORE or SBDC office named. The record log has a first real or practice entry with a receipt. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should a good business record include?
options: Date, who, what and how much, with receipts
Only the total for the year
check.why: Clear records with receipts help at tax time and show how the business is doing.

check.q: You get paid for a cleaning job in cash. What would you do?
options: Keep no record because it is cash
Record it, put it in your business account and set some aside for taxes
Put it in a friend's account
check.why: Recording income, keeping business money separate and saving for taxes keeps you out of trouble.
